As the pushback over Portland public
schools proposed school closures
continues, tonight Irvington elementary
parents tell K12 they're still waiting
for some clear answers and they're also
accusing the district of moving too
fast. This comes after Governor Kotek
urged the district to slow down, but the
district says it does need to act to
preserve student services. K12's Thumby
Varma is live at Irvington Elementary
School tonight. So Thumby, the
superintendent met with those parents
today there at the school. How did they
feel about it?
>> They were really happy to meet with the
superintendent, but they still believe
that there's so much to unpack and not
enough time to do so. For example, they
mentioned that they learned about this
proposal just this month, but that the
board is going to vote on it by the end
of this calendar year and with so many
big questions about student quality of
life, they need more time. Remember, up
to 14 schools could be closed and
students from those schools would be
sent to other nearby schools. Today we
spoke to several parents who explained
to us what they want to see from the
district before any final decisions.
>> That turnaround feels extremely fast and
it's not just about listening, it's
about partnership.
>> And we say, "Well, what does happens
when you close our school and merge it
with another school? What what do we
get? What kind of extra resources does
that look like?"
>> But we're not exactly sure how this
solves the problem. Uh there's a lot of
data out there nationwide that shows
that these kinds of closures don't
address what is being said is the
problem.
>> I'm against uh how
you know,
how kind of how kind of opaque the
process has been and the conclusions
that are being drawn.
>> In a statement, Portland Public Schools
emphasizes their commitment to hearing
families out. They note that they've had
over 50 community engagement sessions
where they can really provide some
answers to the families. They also
explain how moving fast is important to
protect student services that could be
lost due to declining enrollment, which
also means declining funding. And the
district says those listening sessions
started in March, though families
learned about the right-sizing proposal
this month. The district says there are
also more events for parents to voice
out their concerns. To see when and
where those are, you can go to our
website at katu.com. Reporting live in
Northeast Portland, Tanvi Verma, K2
News.

this process, the district has been
hosting engagement opportunities with
the public for months, more than 50
district-wide so far. Here are just a

the next week with more on the calendar
